Getting started with FGstab

getting-started.Rmd

Overview

FGstab implements Integrated Path Stability Selection (IPSS) for high-dimensional variable selection in the Fine-Gray competing risks regression model. The method extends the stability selection framework of Meinshausen & Bühlmann (2010) to the penalised Fine-Gray estimator.

The core idea is simple: instead of fitting a single LASSO model, the data is repeatedly split in half and a LASSO Fine-Gray model is fitted on each half-sample across a grid of regularisation values λ\lambda. The selection frequency of each feature — the proportion of half-samples in which it receives a non-zero coefficient — is tracked along the path. Features that are consistently selected across many subsamples and many values of λ\lambda are considered reliable.

Installation

fastcmprsk is required but not on CRAN — install it from GitHub first:

remotes::install_github("erickawaguchi/fastcmprsk")

Then install FGstab:

remotes::install_github("hugocannafarina/FGstab")
library(FGstab)

Simulating competing risks data

sim_competing() generates synthetic data from the Fine-Gray model with a user-controlled covariance structure. We use the independent design here for simplicity.

set.seed(42)
dat <- sim_competing(
  n_ind       = 200,
  n_pred      = 10,
  n_var       = 300,
  design      = "independent",
  censor_rate = 0.3
)

# dat$X               — covariate matrix (200 x 300), centred and scaled
# dat$surv            — data frame: Tobs, evtype (0/1/2), id
# dat$true_pred_index — indices of the 10 truly predictive features
# dat$beta            — true coefficient vector

table(dat$surv$evtype)
#> 
#>  0  1  2 
#> 60 81 59

The outcome matrix y passed to FGstab() must have two columns: observed time and event type (0 = censored, 1 = event of interest, 2 = competing event).

y <- cbind(time = dat$surv$Tobs, status = dat$surv$evtype)

The IPSS method

Stability paths

For each of B=100B = 100 subsampling iterations, the data is split into two halves of size ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2 \rfloor. On each half, a LASSO Fine-Gray model is fitted over a grid of λ\lambda values from λmax\lambda_{\max} (no feature selected) down to 0.05⋅λmax0.05 \cdot \lambda_{\max}. The selection frequency of feature jj at regularisation parameter λ\lambda is:

Π̂j(λ)=12B∑k=12B𝟏[β̂j(k)(λ)≠0] \hat{\Pi}_j(\lambda) = \frac{1}{2B} \sum_{k=1}^{2B} \mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{\beta}_j^{(k)}(\lambda) \neq 0\right]

Plotting Π̂j(λ)\hat{\Pi}_j(\lambda) against 1/λ1/\lambda yields the stability path of feature jj. Features with high maximum selection probability across the path are most reliably associated with the outcome.

IPSS scores and the EFP bound

IPSS integrates the stability paths to produce a score for each feature that upper-bounds the expected number of false positives (EFP). The bound depends on the choice of bounding function hmh_m (controlled by ipss_function):

hm(π)={0if π≤0.5(2π−1)mif π>0.5 h_m(\pi) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \pi \leq 0.5 \\ (2\pi - 1)^m & \text{if } \pi > 0.5 \end{cases}

with m=1m = 1 ("h1"), m=2m = 2 ("h2", default), or m=3m = 3 ("h3"). Higher mm gives a tighter but more conservative bound. The integrated bound is:

EFP̂≤Ψ̂Sj \widehat{\mathrm{EFP}} \leq \frac{\hat{\Psi}}{S_j}

where Ψ̂\hat{\Psi} is the integrated upper bound on the expected number of false positives (a function of BB, pp, and mm), and SjS_j is the integrated stability path of feature jj transformed by hmh_m.

The EFP score of feature jj is defined as:

EFPj=Ψ̂max⁡(Sj,Ψ̂/p) \mathrm{EFP}_j = \frac{\hat{\Psi}}{\max(S_j,\, \hat{\Psi}/p)}

A low EFP score means that selecting feature jj implies a small expected number of false positives in the selected set.

Q-values

Q-values are derived from EFP scores analogously to the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. The q-value of feature jj is the minimum FDR achievable over all selected sets that include feature jj:

qj=mint:EFPt≤EFPjmaxk:EFPk≤tEFPk|{k:EFPk≤t}| q_j = \min_{t \,:\, \mathrm{EFP}_t \leq \mathrm{EFP}_j} \frac{\max_{k:\, \mathrm{EFP}_k \leq t} \mathrm{EFP}_k}{|\{k : \mathrm{EFP}_k \leq t\}|}

Running FGstab

Inspect scores without selecting 

res <- FGstab(
  X             = dat$X,
  y             = y,
  n_alphas      = 15,
  ipss_function = "h2",
  n_jobs        = 1        # set higher in practice
)
print(res)
#> === FGstab Result (IPSS) ===
#> Features tested  : 300 
#> Features selected: 9 
#> Selected indices : 13, 16, 36, 40, 192, 212, 234, 255, 288

The result contains efp_scores and q_values for all features, which you can inspect before choosing a threshold:

# 10 most stable features (lowest EFP scores)
efp_sorted <- sort(unlist(res$efp_scores))
head(round(efp_sorted, 4), 10)
#>    288     36    255     16     13     40    234    192    212    175 
#> 0.0735 0.0807 0.0846 0.1556 0.1688 0.2950 0.3209 0.3310 0.5536 5.6708

Controlling the expected number of false positives

Setting target_fp = 1 selects all features whose EFP score is at most 1, meaning that at most 1 false positive is expected in the selected set on average.

res_fp <- FGstab(dat$X, y, n_alphas = 15, target_fp = 1, n_jobs = 1)
print(res_fp)
#> === FGstab Result (IPSS) ===
#> Features tested  : 300 
#> Features selected: 9 
#> Selected indices : 13, 16, 36, 40, 192, 212, 234, 255, 288

# How many true positives did we recover?
tp <- sum(res_fp$selected_features %in% dat$true_pred_index)
fp <- length(res_fp$selected_features) - tp
cat("True positives :", tp, "\n")
#> True positives : 8
cat("False positives:", fp, "\n")
#> False positives: 1

Controlling the FDR

Setting target_fdr = 0.2 selects features whose q-value is at most 0.2.

res_fdr <- FGstab(dat$X, y, n_alphas = 15, target_fdr = 0.2, n_jobs = 1)
summary(res_fdr)
#> === Summary: FGstab Result (IPSS) ===
#> Features tested        : 300 
#> Regularisation steps   : 13 
#> Features selected      : 9 
#> 
#> EFP scores (top 10 most stable features):
#>    288     36    255     16     13     40    192    234    212    175 
#> 0.0725 0.0818 0.0863 0.1660 0.1914 0.2629 0.2768 0.4365 0.5935 4.9379 
#> 
#> Q-values (selected features):
#>     13     16     36     40    192    212    234    255    288 
#> 0.0383 0.0383 0.0288 0.0395 0.0395 0.0659 0.0546 0.0288 0.0288

Standard survival data (Cox model)

When there are no competing events, FGstab() is equivalent to IPSS for the penalised Cox model. Use sim_survival() to simulate data in that setting — the output format is identical to sim_competing() but evtype only takes values 0 (censored) and 1 (event).

dat_cox <- sim_survival(n_ind = 200, n_pred = 10, n_var = 300,
                        design = "independent")
y_cox   <- as.matrix(dat_cox$surv[, c("Tobs", "evtype")])

res_cox <- FGstab(dat_cox$X, y_cox, n_alphas = 15, target_fdr = 0.2, n_jobs = 1)
print(res_cox)
#> === FGstab Result (IPSS) ===
#> Features tested  : 300 
#> Features selected: 7 
#> Selected indices : 52, 54, 59, 62, 135, 158, 196

Visualising stability paths

plot() displays the stability paths of all features. Selected features are highlighted in red; the top-5 most stable features are labelled on the right margin.

plot(res_fdr)
#> Error in `ggplot()`:
#> ! impossible de trouver la fonction "ggplot"

You can increase n_highlight to label more features, or save the plot:

p <- plot(res_fdr, n_highlight = 10)
ggplot2::ggsave("stability_paths.pdf", p, width = 8, height = 5)

Covariance structures in sim_competing

sim_competing() supports three designs for the covariate matrix X∼𝒩(0,Σ)X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma):

Design Σjk\Sigma_{jk}
"independent" 𝐈p\mathbf{I}_p
"toeplitz" ρ|j−k|\rho^{|j-k|}
"block" 0.5 within blocks of size 10, 0 otherwise 
dat_toep <- sim_competing(n_ind = 200, n_pred = 10, n_var = 300,
                          design = "toeplitz", rho = 0.7)

Choosing ipss_function

The three bounding functions differ in conservatism:

ipss_function mm Behaviour
"h1" 1 Least conservative, selects more features
"h2" 2 Default, good balance
"h3" 3 Most conservative, selects fewer features

In practice, "h2" is a robust default. Use "h3" if you want to be more stringent, or "h1" if the signal is weak and you can tolerate more false positives.

References

  • Melikechi, O. & Miller, J. W. (2026). Integrated path stability selection. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 121(553), 454–464.
  • Meinshausen, N. & Bühlmann, P. (2010). Stability selection. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 72(4), 417–473.
  • Fine, J. P. & Gray, R. J. (1999). A proportional hazards model for the subdistribution of a competing risk. JASA, 94(446), 496–509.
